THE 

VICE-PRESIDENT’S 

PAGE 


Not possessing a talent for writing, 
but rather, like most of my sex, having 
a passion for talking, I wondered if I 
might have a onesided chat with some 
of you about camping. 

As a former camper, director, com¬ 
mittee member and parent of three 
campers, I have pondered this question 
—what makes the difference between 
a camp that is successful and one that 
is not so successful as a parent or 
onlooker might judge it? Or for that 
matter as the counsellors or campers 
might remember it as they grow older. 
By successful I do not mean financially; 
or with the greatest number of cam¬ 
pers; or the most swimming awards 
won; or even a fine campsite. Let us 
ask ourselves some questions about our 
camp or camps, and try to see our¬ 
selves as others see us. 

For instance, questions about the 
camp might be: 

a) Is the camp well marked for 
parents to locate it? 

b) Is there a place designated for 
parking, safely away from cam¬ 
pers’ activities? 

c) Do visitors receive a friendly 
greeting? 

d) Does the camp appear well-cared 
for, for instance: is adequate at¬ 
tention given to safety — broken 
glass, rusty nails, broken boards 
in floors, torn screens etc.? 

And so on! 


WHAT MAKES THE 

DIFFERENCE— 

by Betty Campbell , 

President, 

Nova Scotia Camping, Association 


Such questions about the campers and 
programme might be: 

a) Have the campers and counsellors 
gone home physically tired out— 
with throats sore from husky 
yelling instead of singing? 

b) Have they taken at least reason¬ 
able care of their belongings? Or 
maybe they have worn only one 
set of underwear for ten days or 
two weeks. Or perhaps lost some 
of their things that possibly the 
family have sacrified to supply. 

c) Have their manners gone un¬ 
checked and in order to get their 
share at meals have they had to 
grab? 

d) Has every camper had a fair and 
equal opportunity to learn skills 
in say baseball, archery etc.? 

Now in this preplanning period is 
the time to reflect on all these things. 
I like to think in terms of operating 
our camps that we have a Code. The 
letter “C” to represent CAUTION — 
the very important caution or care that 
must be taken to preserve life and 
health. The adherence to the health 
rules for nutrition, drinking, water, 
sanitation, fire precautions with fire 
drills practised regularly. Waterfront 
and swimming regulations stricly fol¬ 
lowed at all times for all at camp. 

The letter “O” to stand for ORDER 
—“A place for everything and every¬ 
thing in its place”. All equipment put 
turn to page 175

Canadian Camping 



CAMPING IMPERATIVES 
FOR THE FUTURE 


by Howard G. Gibbs, 

Director—Programme Services, 
Boys* Clubs of America, 

New York City 


Presented at the Ontario Camping Association Convention, 1964 


Not too many years from now this 
city, this province, this nation and 
mine, this world, and probably the 
outer world will be peopled by those 
whose ideas and attitudes and beliefs 
and values and prejudices and toler¬ 
ances and strengths and weakness are 
being developed and nurtured now. 
Today. By us ... as citizens, as 
parents, as professionals in the human 
relations arena. 

Fascination with future is under¬ 
standable but the crystal-ball gazing 
you’ve asked from me is risky business. 
Today’s fad is tomorrow’s folly. Some 
years ago, the Davy Crockett legend 
was big business; today there are 
warehouses full of unsold Davy Crock¬ 
ett hats. Today, Beatle wigs are “in;” 
hopefully, tomorrow will come soon and 
the Beatles will be “out.” 

A very few years ago (1955) a book 
by MORRIS ERNEST — UTOPIA 
1970 — predicted what we felt then 
was fantastic—orbiting communicative 
satellites; paper-thin TV; clothing of 
synthetic fabrics; moon explorations— 
all predictions which are now either 
reality or near fulfillment. 

A book out just recently — 1975 
AND THE CHANGES TO COME — 


cites evidence of cars guided electron¬ 
ically without drivers; of air-supported 
vehicles; atomic radiated foods elimin¬ 
ating refrigeration; walking will be 
replaced by moving sidewalks; shop¬ 
ping by IBM cards; disposable cloth¬ 
ing; 90 minutes to Europe; 30-hour 
work week; telephones carried in the 
pocket. 

Of course, most of this is concerned 
with “Things;” not people but even 
there we have the prediction that by 
the year 2050, we shall produce a 
breed of monkeys which will be able 
to perform most of the routine tasks 
of life. Today’s CIT may be replaced 
by the MIT—Monkeys-in-Training! 

If you will recognize with me that 
I speak on the assumption that your 
camping scene and mine and your 
children and mine and your country 
and mine have more that is in common 
than is different, I would ask you to 
examine CAMPING IMPERATIVES 
FOR THE FUTURE with these three 
thoughts in mind: 

1. It is imperative that any compas¬ 
sionate, democratic society have 
rules and regulations — which we 
call values. 

2. It is imperative that we not only 


Toronto , Canada, June 1964 


145 



have values but that we are con¬ 
stantly aware and alert to the 
ease with which these values can 
be ignored or distorted. 

3. It is imperative that we not only 
have values and that we are aware 
that they can be easily ignored or 
distorted, but it is also imperative 
that each of us individually and 
collectively in our own way aggres¬ 
sively seeks to translate these values 
into every day practice and action. 

May I, then, take each of these three 
points and examine them: 

a. WE BELIEVE in the dignity 
and importance of each human 
being — that each one counts 
— rich or poor; young or old; 
white or colored; attractive or 
unattractive; regardless of 
language or religion or brains 
or any other characteristic— 
each one counts. 

b. WE BELIEVE that each of us 
is free to act and think as we 
please -as long as we do not 
hurt anyone else’s freedom. 

c. WE BELIEVE that each 
should be able to develop in 
keeping with his abilities. 

d. WE BELIEVE that the family 
is our basic social institution. 

e. WE BELIEVE that groups are 
powerful influences (for either 
good or evil). 

f. WE BELIEVE in change as 
imperative and normal. 

g. WE BELIEVE that each of us 
at all ages has a private and 
personal responsibility to be 
concerned about the welfare of 
others and that this concern 
for others has its roots in 
childhood. 

h. WE BELIEVE in work as a 
normal part of a good life. 

i. WE BELIEVE in play, not as 
a reward for work or freedom 
from work, or escape from 
boredom, or something earned, 


or mere entertainment, but as 
an innate need and right essen¬ 
tial to normal living, 

j. WE BELIEVE that the out-of- 
doors camp is a particularly 
ideal setting to translate these 
other values into reality. 

Secondly, let me call your attention 
to the way we ignore or distort some 
of these values in our current ap¬ 
proaches to child development. 

To put it bluntly and succintly, I 
think we might even ask ourselves at 
times, “Do we really love our 
children?” 

This is a legitimate and serious ques¬ 
tion which can be addressed to us as 
parents, as professionals in youth work, 
as citizens in the compassionate democ¬ 
racy I mentioned, where concern for 
children is one of our great strengths. 

Let me be specific: 

In some of our concepts about rais¬ 
ing young children, particularly in 
middle-class society, we are forcing 
grown-up ways on childhood days — 
the voice is not of the turtle but of the 
rabbit. Everything is speeded up ex¬ 
cept, of course, some important things 
like human relations where progress 
is so slow it makes a snail look speedy. 
We reward the speedy — the fast child 
is smart, the slow child is dull. We do 
not usually ask why we are in a hurry 
or even where we are going. We just 
want to get there. We start children 
in school earlier and earlier (so we can 
have more time to ourselves?)— and 
get them out earlier and earlier—and 
then wail because our young people 
spend so much time away from home 
and marry so soon. In our admirable 
goal to provide for a good adulthood, 
we are bypassing childhood almost as 
though we are all either so prejudiced 
against it or are not really comfortable 
with children or do not really enjoy 


146 


Canadian Camping 



them. We seem to like children best 
when they act like miniature adults. 

Now not only are we bypassing or, 
at least, shortening childhood, we 
appear to be treating children as one 
of our status symbols and looking upon 
parenthood as a competitive sport; 
some of us frustrated athletic fathers 
meet our own needs by forcing big 
league competition on little people... 
some mothers work at motherhood as 
relentlessly as some do at femininity. 
Mom is so “busy” “understanding” 
her children and doing what is good 
for them and, incidentally, competing 
with other mothers, that she hasn’t 
time to enjoy her offspring . . . she is 
what is called the “professional 
mother.” 

Too many parents mistake the 
meaning of “permissiveness” which 
comes from the word “permit” and 
does not mean “to do nothing.” So 
we’re afraid to say “no,” to set limits; 
to be firm about what is right and 
wrong. We end up with a statistical 
approach to children, i.e., if enough 
parents push their children into early 
adulthood, it must be right; this is 
like saying that, since delinquency is 
so common, every home should have 
a delinquent! It is no wonder children 
can use the so-effective dodge, “But, 
Dad. eveiyone else is doing it.” 

I call your attention to a recent book 
— THE CHILD WORSHIPPERS by 
MARGARET LEAR. Read it, if only 
because you ought to be prepared to 
react to the chapter on camps entitled 
SNAKEBITE IS NOT THE PROB¬ 
LEM — a witty but caustic and some¬ 
what bitter, too-glib account of a camp 
as a summer resting place for over¬ 
privileged children. You and I know 
better. Camps are lambasted in this 
chapter, mainly because the author 
feels many have not fought hard 
enough to keep the outdoors in camp¬ 


ing, and she has a point there. (It 
was most encouraging to see that your 
Conference here really emphasized the 
out-of-doors.) You will have difficulty 
with her description of camps as a sum¬ 
mer resort with and without wall-to-wall 
carpeting; at the charge that many 
parents chose camps more because of 
high fees than high quality (nothing 
is too good for our Billy!); at the 
description of camp programmes 
wherein so-called real camping consists 
of a safari by station wagon to a bar¬ 
becue pit presided over by the camp 
chef. 

These descriptions are, of course, 
accompanied by some more palatable 
statements but the overall impression 
bears out the theme of the book . . . 
that far too many parents are using 
their children to satisfy their own 
need for status and that too many 
camps perpetuate this approach to 
child-rearing by giving parents what 
they want, not necessarily what is good 
for children. 

■K- # # 

You’ll recall one of the values 1 
mentioned indicated the importance of 
helping each child develop within his 
capacity to grow. What I have just 
mentioned ignores this value, in the 
same way that, with teenagers, we have 
distorted the goal of human dignity. 

Not only are we seducing young 
children away from childhood but with 
the teens we have created a whole 
new and essentially unhealthy culture. 
Here there is not a question of using 
the young as status symbols; we’re 
talking about the creation of a way of 
life, created in a large part by adults, 
often for commercial reasons. 

We, who profess to love our youth, 
have built up and/or permitted such 
an essentially unhealthy, often ma¬ 
terialistic, culture, that the term “teen” 
has become almost a dirty word. For 
some, we are so busy creating an early 


Toronto , Canada , June 1964 


147 



facade of sophistication that it is no 
wonder they too often become minia¬ 
ture conforming organization men. For 
others, we create great confusion by 
either telling them to go “Find your¬ 
self,” or “Get lost.” We get impatient 
and ask them, “Why don’t you grow 
up?” and, when they do makes noises 
like a budding adult, we tell them, 
“You’re getting too big for your 
britches.” We, either refuse to recog¬ 
nize capacities or, else, we ask too 
much of them. We either try to keep 
them as teens too long as an antidote 
to what we have done in taking their 
childhood away, or else we try to 
make them part of the adult establish¬ 
ment too soon. We forget that adoles¬ 
cence is the proving ground for 
adulthood; it is the time when rebellion 
is normal, not abnormal; when quest¬ 
ioning is to be encouraged, not dis¬ 
couraged; when often irresponsible 
youth begins to be responsible. 

What I am trying to say is that we 
ought to carefully separate the normal, 
natural stage of life called adolescence, 
from the abnormal, artificial, adult- 
made new profession called 
teenage-ism. 

Let me mention that bypassing child¬ 
hood and the current approach to 
teens is paying unfortunate dividends 
in our college generation. In my 
country, half of America’s college stu¬ 
dents either quit or flunk before grad¬ 
uation; an appalling number suffer 
from emotional and psychosomatic 
disorders; and the suicide rate is rising 
dramatically. 

Lastly, my third area for discussion 
concerns what we can do, individually 
and collectively, to protect our values 
and to aggressively translate them into 
practice. 

Specifically, let me be presumptuous 
enough to make some suggestions re¬ 
lated to our interest in camping. These 
are based not just on what we could 
do, but what many are doing. 


1. It is imperative that we help 
revive childhood ... I am not saying 
prolong childhood or revere it ... I 
am saying revive it. 

2. What I am saying is that we, at 
camp, can make very sure that we are 
not part of this headlong rush to push 
children beyond their years. A child’s 
best way of learning is in the concrete 
. . . not abstract . . . through first-hand 
experience . . . through exploration. 
In camp, we have the setting for just 
such experiences at a pace geared to 
the needs and interests of children. 

THIS MEANS that competition in 
camp will be to improve a child not 
prove how skilled the athletic direc¬ 
tor is. 

THIS MEANS that the physical and 
mental capacities of each child are con¬ 
sidered in groupings and in program- 
ming. 

THIS MEANS that outdoor play, 
particularly for young children, just 
plain fun play, will be the central fact 
of camp life. This means that for teens 
play will be more rugged and challeng¬ 
ing and different. Through play, a 
person will learn to appreciate himself 
and others; will learn that the world 
is beautiful and rough; will learn that 
play is not just with the body but with 
words and tears and smiles or, as 
LAWRENCE FRANK wrote, “Play is 
the way a child learns what no one 
else can teach him.” 

Time for play is important and in¬ 
creasingly available at all ages. The 
person who lives to be 70 will spend 
10 years of that in Sundays, 10 years 
in Saturdays, not to mention holidays. 
When a 30- or 35-hour week comes, 
literally half of our life will be spent 
not working. The great goal of camp¬ 
ing might well be to prepare us for 
the creative use of such leisure. This 
is one of the reasons why camp pro¬ 
grammes have to be varied, have carry¬ 
over activities and not be just the 
same old things repeated year after 
year. 


148 


Canadian Camping 




2. It is imperative that we stress 
our role in helping parents with the 
perplexing business of raising children. 

The great majority of parents are 
loving, concerned human beings. Un¬ 
fortunately, some of the trends in 
child-rearing I have just discussed are 
confusing and more harmful than help¬ 
ful to children. Parents need help and 
it is legitimate for them to seek and 
use such help. 

People such as us in youth work, 
who are skilled with children and who 
get to know parents, are often in a 
position to utilize these relationships in 
helping parents better cope with the 
problems of child-rearing. 

We can help parents see the dangers 
of too much pressure on children (at 
home, in school, in the community, in 
church,) and we can certainly make 
sure that camp is a place where repose 
is reputable. 

We can help parents see the danger 
of demanding perfection — note I 
said perfection not excellence. Living 
up to one’s capacities is not the same 
as being forced to do the impossible, 
nor can one live up to capacity every 
day, all day. I am -all for tailoring 
education to the intellectual and social 
capacities of individuals but I am also 
for recognizing that children are not 
machines and, therefore, they need a 
change of pace. 

One of the understandable goals of 
parents is to have our children be what 
we were not . . . but the pressure to¬ 
ward perfection today has unfortunate 
byproducts—i.e., it may well be the 
cause of so much cheating *at schools 
where the passing of exams is more 
important than the joy of learning; 
some of the dropouts among middle- 
class children may well be caused by 
those who cannot achieve by hook or 
crook . . so they quit; similarly, in 
camp, we battle to interpret to those 
parents whose idea of learning is based 


only on skills learned, that genuine 
education includes helping children be¬ 
come independent beings and indepen¬ 
dent learners; that proficiency in skills 
grows out of working hard and that 
self-satisfaction can be as important «as 
skills itself. 

We can help parents see that every¬ 
one has his failures and that helping 
children accept mistakes is part of 
growing up. 

We can help parents realize the im¬ 
portance of limits. Parents who really 
love their children are also willing to 
limit them in order to help them grow. 
Children even want to be limited, to 
know where they stand. Sometimes, 
it is the parent’s duty and job to be 
a heel; sometimes children want to be 
able to blame what they do not want 
to do anyway on their parents. Some¬ 
times children do not want to do what 
everyone else is doing and are relieved 
to have a willing scapegoat. But we can 
limit in camps, too. We must be more 
than just “pals.” There is power in 
the positive “no.” 

We can also help parents see that 
it is part of growing up for our youth 
to look at others outside the home for 
their ideas and values and examples 
and that the camp counsellor who 
seems to be so all-important is a valu¬ 
able ally, not a competitive threat to 
parenthood. Sometimes our counsellors 
do not realize their influence is year- 
round. 

We can also help parents realize that 
the problems of child-raising are not 
settled by some magic formula; that 
there are times to disregard as well as 
regard the experts; that one’s own 
judgment may be sharpened by some 
attention to the views of the specialists 
but that, in the long haul, there is no 
substitute for instinct; that if children 
know where they stand, they also know 
they are cared about as well as cared 
for and, therefore, are truly loved. 


Toronto , Canada , June 1964 


149 



3. It is imperative that we realize 
that camping is education, not just as 
a claim, but as our aim, not as fantasy 
but as fact. 

It is important for us to use knowl¬ 
edge of the way children develop so 
that we can demonstrate that educa¬ 
tion is not the monopoly of the school¬ 
room setting; that education is not 
just facts but thoughts; that children 
learn by knowing themselves as well 
as the three “R’s”; that children learn 
both by living peacefully with others 
and by healthy friction; that children 
learn by historical knowledge of pre¬ 
vious discoveries and by their own 
awakenings; that children learn by 
adapting to the new as well as using 
the usual; that there are subjects which 
can be best learned in a camp setting; 
that camping is education in a different 
setting with an unique contribution to 
make, not in competition with the 
classroom as an ally. 

Education is not confined to a class¬ 
room; education is a continuing process 
found in many settings. 

Education is not only the mission of 
the teacher in the school; education is 
the mission of parents, of the leisure¬ 
time guide, of the religious leader and 
of the group professional. The teacher 
in camp does not cease to be a teacher 
when he leaves the classroom. 

Education is not just skills of the 
intellect; education includes physical 
health and spiritual well-being and 
emotional stability and social growth. 

If you can accept these statements, 
then a major goal for us all is not to 
ask, “Are we educators?” for we are 
and must be; we might better con¬ 
centrate on “What kind and quality 
of educator are we?” 

This question is easier asked than 
answered. 

It might be said that our professional 
difficulty is the difficulty in being pro¬ 
fessional. 


As professionals, perhaps we 

should have 

.... less worry about empty spaces in 
camp and more concern about 
empty spaces in children’s hearts 
and minds; 

.... less status-centered programmes 

and more emphasis on the out-of- 

doors as the central core of 
camping; 

.... less city-type athletics and more 
out-of-doors aesthetics; 

.... less “busy-work” -and more crea¬ 
tive play; 

. . . . less preoccupation with “know¬ 

how” and more occupation with 
“know-why.” 

.... less concentration on the trivial 
routines and more irritation with 
signs of intolerance and prejudice; 
.... less abject, automatic submission 
to parent’s demands and more 
able interpretation that we are 
skilled allies; possessing special 
training and experience which will 
help them and their children; 
.... less thinking of camp as a sanc¬ 
tuary from life and more as an 
educational gateway to life; 

It might be said also that for many 
of us our principal confusion is the 
confusion of our principles. 

Perhaps all of us should be a little 
less comfortable about our material 
well-being and more uncomfortable 
about the social ills which affect all our 
children; 

.... less pushing of children into early 
maturity and more pacing of 
children’s progress by stages; 

.... less teaching our children to love 
things and use people and more 
teaching them to love people and 
use things; 

.... less insistence on perfection in 
children and more recognition 
that mistakes are expected and 
•accepted; 


150 


Canadian Camping 



.... less filling our own adult needs 
for status and more fulfilling the 
needs of children to be children; 

.... less adult abdication of authority 
and more recognition that adults 
have rights too; 

.... less acceptance of the world as it 
is and more attempts to change 
it for the better; 

.... less trying to fit our youth into 
society and more trying to make 
a society fit for youth. 

Perhaps the greatest imperative, 
therefore, is less undue concern about 
what the future holds and more due 
concern about the children who hold 
the future. 

As we approach this summer, I hope 
it will be one where we truly try to 
help our campers: 

Enjoy their play 
Nurture their needs 
Discover their talents 
Broaden their viewpoints 
Set their goals 
Strengthen their character 
Form their values 
Accent their positives 
Live with their negatives 
Adjust to their limitations 
Appreciate others 
Understand themselves. 

I hope that the imperatives for this 
summer will be that every camp be¬ 
comes a citadel of care and love in a 
world which too often either does not 
really care or cares in the wrong way 
or cares for the wrong reasons or loves 
carelessly instead of carefully. 

For I end with my beginning: 

Not too many years from now this 
city, this province, this nation and 
mine, this world and probably the 
outer world will be peopled by those 
whose ideas and attitudes and beliefs 
and values and prejudices and toler¬ 
ances are being developed and nur¬ 
tured now. Today. By us. 

—•

Hey-Ho! 
Up the Creek 
We Go 

by P. M. Taschereau, Naturalist > 
Nova Scotia Museum of Science and 
Woodland Boys’ Camp , Quebec 


Woodland Camp has a very muddy 
stream. 

For many years it merely marked 
the boundary beyond which young 
campers might not go without their 
leader. Then one year a model boat 
race was held and young campers 
flocked to its banks as never before. 
Many at this time dared its clouded 
waters and found it not so deep and 
unpleasant as expected. 

, It was several years -after this that 
a fertile and sympathetic; imagination 
conceived of the “Mudpuppy Society”. 
This institution, whose members had 
passed the entrance requirements by a; 
certain nature hike*.brought campers; 
a step , further from the banks of . the 
creek—right, into the middle of it! ; 

■? Considered a select activity for a ! 
chosen few, a mudpuppy hiking group i 
consisted of two to six boys—some of j 
them timid or homesick, some of them 
keen nature enthusiasts and one or 
two leaders., They met during Tree 
time under the shade of a large ash 
tree by the creek’s edge. As the seated 
group (wearing short pants, or bathing 
suits) removed; shoes and socks, the 
all important rtiles were explained by 
the leaders. 

f 

The rules were these: 

1. Once, in the creek no foot must leave 



its watery element to mar the muddy 
bank. (The reason given for this 
rule was that important nature signs, 
animal tracks and trails height be 
obscured or obliterated by human 
foot marks.) ; 

2. The group must 'stay close 5 together 
with a leader in front and one be¬ 
hind. On no account are ‘ Hikers 
allowed ahead of the first Trader. 
Slipping (too often) is a disgrace 
though" never disqualifying. 

3. There must Be general quiet..' and 
talk must be only of. observations 
and creek life. (If . they were' suf¬ 
ficiently quiet, that muskrat ‘ occa¬ 
sionally seen might be surprised 
around the next bend)' 

4. The leaders would* point out things 
of interest along , the-.way up. to the 

, place of:return.. On the, return trip 
the hikers must point out these 
things to the leaders.- 

Our route meandered from the ash 
tree to an old log bridge, (perhaps a 
thousand feet in a straight line.) Some 
of the things the mudpuppies saw, did 
and learned were: 

—At numerous points along the shore 
were beautiful records of “little 
brother to the bear’—the tracks of 
raccoon. 

—Bird tracks abounded, along with 
soft pellets that we later, decided 
were their droppings. 


152 


Canadian Camping 






—Once as we sat on the shore after 
a hike we were rewarded by the 
sight of a monstrous snapping turtle. 
It was ambling downstream just 
underwater and breaking the surface 
like a bobbing piece of algae- 
covered dead-wood. 

—Frogs were everywhere. Bullfrogs 
were distinguished from Greenfrogs 
and the difference between male 
and female Greenfrog were learned. 
Some frogs were caught, observed 
and then released so that we might 
watch their swimming and escape 
tactics. 

—Canada mint was tasted, the float¬ 
ing bladders of the seed of Garex 
sedges explained and the trailing 
pennies of Moneywart and tall 
purple stands of Loosestrife pointed 
out. 

—The “wet feet* habitat preference of 
Alder, Silver maple, Sensitive fern 
and others was observed. 

—The formation of ox-bows, a geo¬ 
logical process, was seen in action. 

—It was found that where the stream 
flowed most swiftly the bottom was 
usually firm (and often slippery as 
many personally demonstrated). In 
the quieter, slower moving parts, 
the pleasant, cool mud oozed be¬ 
tween our toes and we sank often 
to ankle depth. 

*—But it w»as at the log bridge, the 
point of rest and return, that the 
greatest of mysteries lay.—There, in 
a cleft of bark could be seen the shed 
skin of a garter snake exactly where 
the snake had crawled in to free 
himself! Though the skin is no 
longer there, the repetition of its 
story is now part of the firmly estab¬ 
lished tradition of mudpuppy lore. 
Perhaps someday an obliging snake 
will again choose this site to shed its 
skin, later to be discovered by some 
keen young eyes. 

On the trip back to the tree the 
order was the same except that this 
time the campers must point out to 


the leaders the intricacies of creek 
nature. 

The person first sighting a plant or 
nature sign he recognized, called it out 
for leader and group to hear. For the 
name he received a mark and for 
telling something about its natural his¬ 
tory, another mark. A mark was 
similarly deducted for each mistake 
thereby lessening the amount of guess¬ 
ing. If the same species of plant came 
into sight again around a bend, the 
name could be repeated. Thus, even 
those who seemed able to recall very 
little of what was pointed out on the 
up stream trip, by dint of the excited 
repetition of names by others (as their 
scores mounted), were soon able to 
identify many finds. 

Each kept his own score which was 
recorded, as shoes and socks were re¬ 
placed and we hurried off* to a swim 
or meal. No one was informed at this 
time whether he had passed or failed. 
This knowledge was withheld until the 
last council fire. 



We met on a few other occasions to 
practice the “Mudpuppy Song” 

—“Hey ho, up the creek we go; 
Necturi maculosi 
Through the mud and muck 
we go, ho ho ho . . . Hey ho 
(etc.)” (fading out) 

This was sung to the tune of the 
Gypsy Wanderers’—“Hey ho nobody 
home etc.’’ The scientific name of the

CANOE SAFETY 

PRACTICES 

AND PROCEDURES 


The following statement of canoe¬ 
ing practices is, in part, the result of 
a summary derived from the sub¬ 
missions of a number of Canadian 
camps. These had been requested in 
reference to the Department of Trans¬ 
port legislation proposals regarding the 
use of life-jackets in canoes. In present¬ 
ing the minimum standards or recom¬ 
mendations for canoe safety, it is to 
be hoped that all camps will review 
their own practices and communicate 
with the Ontario Camping Association 
either to approve, or to suggest im¬ 
provement of the various points made. 

It is recognized that any set of prac¬ 
tices is governed in its application by 
a number of variables. The size of the 
lake and its general characteristics 
must be taken into consideration, as 
must the prevailing wind, the depth 
and turbidity of the water in the 
paddling area, the presence or absence 
of currents, the age of the campers 
and their ability, the presence of motor 
boats and other heavy water traffic, 
the wind and weather conditions, ex¬ 
perience and ability of instructors. All 
these must be considered, as they have 
a distinct bearing on the safety pro¬ 
cedures adopted in a canoeing pro¬ 
gramme. 

Generally there are three considera¬ 
tions for canoeing safety; swimming 


prerequisites; conduct of canoeing pro¬ 
gramme and regulations and agree¬ 
ments relevant to canoe tripping. 

A. Swimming prerequisities: 

1. Campers who swim less than one 
hundred yards but more than 
twenty, may paddle in a restricted 
area with a staff member. Life 
jackets ought to be worn if the 
area is over three feet deep. 

2. Campers who swim more than one 
hundred yards may paddle within 
•a restricted area with another 
camper of at least the same ability. 

•3. Campers who swim two hundred 
yards or more may paddle singly. 

4. Campers who paddle three to a 
canoe ought to have one member 
who swims two hundred yards 
and the other two at least one 
hundred yards each. 

5. Passengers in canoes should be 
able to swim one hundred yards. 
If a qualified staff member is in 
the canoe the passenger may swim 
not less than twenty-five yards 
provided that a life-jacket is avail¬ 
able in the canoe. 

B. General Safety Procedures for 

Canoeing: 

1. Canoes should not be taken out 
unless permission has been given 
by a member of the waterfront 
staff. 


154 


Canadian Camping 



2. Canoes should not be taken out 
until a responsible staff member is 
on duty. 

3. Canoeing should be conducted in 
a prescribed area which can be 
observed at all times by an area 
guard or supervisor. Exceptions 
may be made for advanced padd- 
lers, by special arrangement. 

4. At -all times, a checking system 
should be enforced so that a staff 
member knows which canoes are 
out and who is in each canoe. 
(Canoes may be numbered and 
campers wear identification tags.) 

5. Canoeing should not be permitted 
at night or during hazardous con¬ 
ditions as in stormy weather. 

6. Safety practices ought to be ob¬ 
served by staff and campers, in 
recreational periods as well as in 
instructional classes. 

7. Load limits for canoes ought to 
be taught and enforced. 

8. The jjse of the canoe as a rescue 
device ought to be known to all 
campers and . staff. . 

9. During free and recreational can¬ 
oeing, patrols in canoes or other 
suitable craft, and overall area 
guards, must be on duty. 

10. Proper clothing including sensible 
footwear must be worn (Rubber 
boots or large leather boots cannot 
be permitted). 

11. To learn and practise special skills 
such as gunwaling, shakeouts, 
canoe awash or stunts, a camper 
ought to have a partner and the 
permission of the responsible 
waterfront staff member on duty. 

C. Safety Procedures for Canoe 
Trips 

1. To go on a canoe trip, a camper 
ought to have the following swim¬ 
ming and rescue skills: 

a. Swim two hundred yards 
free style. 


b. Swim fifty yards with 
clothes and footwear and 
then remove them in deep 
water. 

c. Upset a canoe, hang on for a 
reasonable period and then 
demonstrate how the canoe 
may be used as a rescue 
device assuming no other 
help is available. 

d. With -assistance perform a 
canoe over canoe rescue. 

e. Demonstrate drownproofing 
or treading water for five 
minutes. 

2. Before launching on a trip, campers 
ought to have the following ex¬ 
periences: 

a. Paddling under windy con¬ 
ditions. 

b. Paddling along streams and 
swifts. 

c. Physical fitness preparation 
for portaging, pack carrying, 
and long periods of paddling. 

3. The trip leader and assisting staff 
members should have a clear 
agreement with the camp on the 
following points: 

a. Where the trip will be each 
day. 

.; b. Procedure for extreme 
weather conditions, injury 
and illness. 

c. Bases for making judgments 
in swift water conditions. 

d. P r a c t i c e s for swimming 
along canoe trip routes. 

e. Full knowledge of the haz¬ 
ardous conditions which 
exist along canoe routes 
used. 

4. Up to the age of about fourteen, 
campers should generally serve as 
bowmen or middlemen rather than 
sternsmen, unless conditions are 
such that changing positions may 
be considered safe and practical.

Programme 
FOR SHORT- TERM 

What do vve mean by short-term 
camping? Some of us operate for a 
full summer with the same programme 
staff and have different groups of 
campers come and go for one, two or 
three-week camping periods. Others 
take a church or an agency group to a 
camp for a one or two-week period, 
attending for the same period with 
their campers. The variable lies in the 
continuity of staff and the length of 
the camping period. 

We hear various people talking at 
various times about the advantages 
and disadvantages of one camping 
period over another. “To run a suc¬ 
cessful camp you must have the 
campers for at least six weeks”: “In 
one week you just begin to know the 
campers and get started on some 
worthwhile activities when they leave 
you”! 

“Anything longer than three weeks 
results in bored campers and staff who 
run out of programme ideas”. All of 
us have heard these complaints and 
many more. But the fact of the matter 
remains whether we have one week or 
six weeks with our campers, they come 
to us with a whole range of needs and 
interests which they hope consciously 
or unconsciously to have satisfied, at 
least in part, by coming to our camp. 
We in turn are camp leaders because 
we have a conviction that these needs 
and interests can in part, be satisfied, 
through the unique experience of 
camping in a child’s life. Therefore, 
our task is to make the best use of the 
time, facilities and staff at our disposal 
in the creation of the best possible 
camping programme. 

We are well aware of the disadvan¬ 
tages of a short-term camp, but let 
us consider some of its advantages. 
First of all, the short-term camp 


by Robert Chandler, 

Camp Boulderwood, 
University Settlement, 

CAMPS Toronto, Ontario 

means that we are able to give a 
camping experience to many more 
campers than would otherwise be pos¬ 
sible. Secondly, leadership may be 
available on a short-term basis but not 
for a full season. This often means 
that for Scouts, Guides, Church 
groups, etc., the same leadership can 
be provided at camp as in town, and 
camping then becomes in a very real 
sense an extension of the city pro¬ 
gramme. Thirdly, the short-term pro¬ 
gramme may not place such great 
demands upon the creativity of the 
young counsellor as does the long-term 
camp. (This must not mean however 
that the quality of leadership can be 
at a lower level.) 

What are some of the pit-falls in 
short-term camping? The first one is 
the temptation to cram every minute 
of every working day full of organized 
activity in an effort to do in two weeks 
what another camp might hesitate to 
do in six. 

Camping should be a relaxed, freely 
organized leisure experience with time 
to watch and think and talk and be 
with each other. If there is no time 
for this programme then the camp has 
not been all that it might be for our 
campers. The second pit-fall is one 
which goes to the other extreme. “The 
period is so short that we just keep 
the campers occupied and not try to 
teach anything or do any projects”. 
A camper can become bored even with 
one day of this approach. The third 
pit-fall is the tendency on the part of 
staff to fall back on what was done 
last period because it takes less creative 
dnergy than thinking up new projects. 
This type of thinking sells the second, 
third and fourth period campers short 
because they are getting a second-hand 
camping experience. This is not to 


156 


Canadian Camping 



say, however, that good projects done 
last period should not be done again 
if they were good and if they seem 
appropriate for these campers, but 
rather that they should not be done 
again just because we are too lazy to 
create new ideas to give to our 
campers. 

Programme is everything that the 
camper does in camp and everything 
we do with the campers. This broad 
interpretation has been made before, 
but I feel that it is of special signifi¬ 
cance to us who are engaged in short¬ 
term camping. From this vantage 
point we cease to look at the swim 
period, the arts and crafts group, the 
overnight hike as the only programme 
activities.,. We begin to see the cabin 
clean-up period,, the informal fifteen 
minutes a counsellor and a camper 
spend on a rock talking together or 
happy conversation in the cabin just 
before lights out as. being every bit as 
much a part of programme and so 
often far jnore meaningful than the 
bjest planned activity. .Programme is 
the camper’s total, experience at camp. 
Whether it is good or bad.,depends 
upon our ability as camp leaders to 
stimulate and involve*' ‘ 6'iir caftipers 
creatively in that experience. 

Who Creates Programme? 

I use tlie word “create” deliberately 
because the effectiveness of 'the camp 
programme depends upon its' creative 
use bfy everybne in cafnp—both staff 
member and ’ camper/ Programme is 
the' technical tool we use in group 
leadership and,” just as the craftsman 
builds a finished product through the 
skilled use of his tools, so we as leaders 
biiild meaningful group relationships, 
help healthy personalities to grow and 
healthy campers to have fun through 
skilled use of our programme tools/* 

The camp director and the pro¬ 
gramme director help create the pro¬ 
gramme by interpreting the camp’s 
policy and objectives to the staff in 
such a way that the staff becomes 
identified with these objectives and 


personally committed to them. The 
provision of adequate facilities for pro¬ 
gramme and opportunities for super¬ 
vision and in-service training and the 
personal involvement of every in¬ 
dividual st-afF member in the operation 
of the camp-as-a-whole are responsi¬ 
bilities of the director. The way in 
which he approaches these tasks in a 
very real sense sets the tone for the 
entire programme. If he is limited, 
rigid and lacking in imagination, then 
the chances are his counsellors will 
be too. 

The activities staff create the pro¬ 
gramme by involving their assistants, 
and the campers interested in their 
particular activity, in the planning of 
the projects or classes and in present¬ 
ing them in an: interesting and stimu T 
lating way. The crafts fpunsellor who 
says “I have decided we , are going v tp 
make driftwood animal s to-day” 
creates, one type of programme * the 
one who [says “Some of you asked, if 
you could make something out of^drift- 
wood today, atfid evei^b^y.JtKdug^Vt^ij 
was a , great. idea” ^creates , another! 
Conpem fpr each camper having a 
satisfying learning experience rather 
than. in, achieving absolute perfectipjo 
should be the key Ao interest group 
activities. ’ , 

; The maintenance, kitchen and healtfi 
staff create programme by, their 
friendly interest in each individual 
camper. In our camp some of the 
more meaningful relationships between 
campers arid staff have been those 
made with service staff. However, fpr 
this to _ happen, maintenance and kit¬ 
chen staff must be made to feel just 
as essential to the camp’s programme 
as the counsellors. 

Section heads create programme 
directly through section events which 
involve both staff and campers in the 
planning process, but more particu¬ 
larly through careful supervision of 
the individual counsellor and G.I.T. 
in the performance of his job. In our 
camp we have found a regular, indi- 


Toronto, Canada, June 1964 


157 



vidual meeting between the section 
head and the cabin staff member to 
be well worth the time involved. Here 
the counsellor knows that the time is 
his for the exclusive discussion of his 
cabin programme and the interacting 
relationships which exist in his cabin. 
He comes to feel in a very real sense 
that his job is the important one in 
camp and, while it is a demanding one, 
he knows that his section head is a 
partner in it. 

The section head’s task, then, is one 
of supporting and reassuring an un¬ 
certain counsellor, limiting an over¬ 
confident one, being a programme 
resource person suggesting leadership 
techniques, and through these roles, he 
develops a type of two-way personal 
relationship between himself and the 
counsellor that we hope oan be estab¬ 
lished in a similar way between coun¬ 
sellor and camper. 

The counsellor is a counsellor in 
every sense of that word. He creates 
programme by careful advance prep¬ 
aration through use of the staff library 
and the knowledge and skills of others 
so that he may stimulate his campers 
in the planning of their own activities. 
In our camp we feel that cabin group 
involvement in the planning of pro¬ 
gramme is every bit as important as 
the activity itself, and it is the skilled 
counsellor who enables his oabin to 
make realistic decisions with respect to 
their own programme. 

Finally, and most important of all, 
the camper himself creates programme. 
He is the reason for it all. He is a 
growing person and as such has the 
right and responsibility to be involved 
in the creation of his own programme 
to the extent of his own ability. A 
camper does not have to be active every 
minute in order to have an effective 
camping experience. A most effective 
cabin programme might be “doing 
nothing” together, with all of the talk¬ 
ing and observing and being together 
that it involves, provided that this is 
what the cabin wants to do, and not 


just the result of poor planning on the 
part of the counsellor. 

Programmes and Objectives 

Objectives are what guide and 
shape the camping programme and 
determine its direction. The camp, its 
campers and their parents all have 
their own objectives for the camping 
experience. 

The camp’s objectives may be giving 
the campers fun, teaching skills, devel¬ 
oping group relationships, providing a 
religious or cultural experience, or a 
combination of any of these and others. 
Whatever the objectives may be, they 
should be identified by the camp and 
interpreted to the staff and campers. 

Campers have objectvies, and these 
are often related to their own indi¬ 
vidual needs—to have fun, to learn to 
swim, canoe or go on trips, to be with 
friends, to get away from parents etc. 
Parents have objectives—to help their 
child learn to make friends, to bring 
him “out of himself’, to learn disci¬ 
pline, to give themselves a rest. All 
these objectives, both positive and neg¬ 
ative, must be recognized by the camp 
in its programme. 

Making Programme Tick 

In summary, the keys to effective 
programming in a short-term camp 
are: recognition by all the staff of the 
inherent advantages and limitations of 
the short-term, determination to make 
it the best possible experience, a cre¬ 
ative attitude on the part of all the 
staff, involvement of both staff and 
campers in the planning, and adequate 
supervision and training opportunities. 
If this is the vantage point from which 
we view our programming, then no 
matter how short our camping period 
may be, we should be successful in 
sending home happy, enthusiastic boys 
and girls, who hopefully are a little 
further along in personality and social 
development, in the ability to have fun 
through group living and in the ac¬ 
quiring of knowledge and skills 
through having been with us.

Canadian Camping 



CAMP SAFETY 


by W. D. Smith, 
President, 

Canadian Camping Association 


Whether resident or family camping, 
many of the accidents that occur could 
be prevented by adequate safety pre¬ 
cautions. The most frequent hazards 
include those found in the normal 
routine of outdoor living. Water, fires, 
poisonous plants, snakes, cutting equip¬ 
ment such as knives and axes, injury 
due to falls, and the resultant panic 
when lost, are some of the dangers that 
should be considered by campers. 
Arrival at Camp 

On arrival at the campsite, campers 
should be made aware of the general 
and specific camp regulations and be 
given a brief tour of the campsite for 
orientation. A well organized and 
supervised first hour at camp does 
much to let the camper know what is 
expected of him and the limitations 
within which he must function in his 
new “home away from home”. Many 
resident camps require a brief medical 
re-check on registration the first day 
of camp in order to bring the pre-camp 
medical examination up to date. At 
the same time, the medical staff record 
and store any supplies brought by the 
camper for individual medication. 
Drinking Water 

Safety regulations regarding drink¬ 
ing water, swimming and boating, open 
fires and the use of axes and knives 
are primary examples of areas of con¬ 
cern in which adequate safety pre¬ 
cautions must be observed. The relative 
importance depends upon the type of 
camping or camp programme in opera¬ 
tion. Drinking water should be tested 
and approved by the local Board of 


Health authority for resident camps. 
On out trips from camp, water may 
be purified by boiling for thirty 
minutes, or the addition of two halo- 
zone tablets per quart -and then allow¬ 
ing it to stand for half an hour. Stream 
or lake pollution, varies with the geo¬ 
graphic location and population 
density. 

Waterfront 

Swimming and boating should be in 
designated areas, supervised, and the 
regulations posted in a prominent place 
both at headquarters and the water¬ 
front area. An established accident 
procedure or routine should be detailed 
and carried out when an emergency 
occurs. For individual safety pre¬ 
cautions, the material on water safety 
available from the Canadian Red Cross 
Society in the brochure “For Your 
Life’s Safe — Read This” is an ex¬ 
cellent reference. Waterfront personnel 
should be at least eighteen years of 
age, have practical experience and be 
certified instructors qualified by the 
Red Cross, Y.M.C.A. or Royal Life 
Saving Society. The ratio of lifeguard 
to swimmer should be one to ten for 
non-swimmers. 

Fires 

Cooking fires and campfires require 
special precautions. Care of fire and 
fire prevention become responsibilities 
of anyone who lights a match in the 
open. A good fire is built in a safe place 
which helps control it; is just large 
enough to serve the need and to make 
thrifty use of wood; is kept under 
control, and is watched at all times;

and, is put out when no longer needed. 
Knives and Axes 

The proper use and maintenance of 
knives and axes is an important phase 
of outdoor living. If the camp is de¬ 
centralized into self-contained units 
where tent or cabin groups cook over 
open fires then instruction in the 
proper and safe use of axes and knives 
is essential. Instruction and practical 
experience forms an integral part of 
in camp training prior to out trips, 
cook outs or overnights. Sharp-edged 
tools are safer to use when kept in 
that condtion so they will not bounce 
or glance off. Edges should be sheathed 
or protected when not in use. 
Poisonous Plants 

There are three poisonous plants 
which could be mistaken for edible 
plants. They are water hemlock, death 
cup mushroom, and baneberry. Water 
hemlock grows from two to four feet 
in height, is a member of the carrot 
family with toothed, three-part purple 
streaked leaves which emit a disagree¬ 
able odour when crushed. It could be 
easily confused with Cow Parsnip or 
Indian Rhubarb which are edible. 
Death Cup Mushroom is found in 
wooded areas, has a soft white cuplike 
formation at the base and a broad 
collar-like ring part way up the stem. 
It has been confused with the common 
edible mushroom. Baneberry is a 
bushy perennial two or three feet tall 
with small white flowers in a short, 
thick terminal cluster. Red or white 
berries replace flowers and resemble 
doll’s eyes in appearance. 

Snakes 

The rattlesnake is found in some of 
the southern areas of the province. It 
exhibits a characteristic pattern of 
dark bands on lighter background that 
is typical. The head is triangle-shaped 
and has a blunt nose. The rattler 
usually gives a warning buzz before 
striking. If bitten keep calm and quiet 
as exercise speeds up circulation and 
spreads the poison. Suction should be 
turn to page ll2

Canadian Camping 


IDEAS — For Programme 

Camp Improvement Day 
Joyce Bertram Camp Ouareau — Quebec 

It simply is NOT true that it never stopped raining in the Laurentians last 
summer, despite all you may have heard to the contrary. It is also not true 
that one camp planted and transplanted so many trees that two of the smaller 
campers lost their way and are there yet. This is the kind of ugly rumour 
which could give camping a bad name! 

It IS true, however, that if a camp director deliberately chooses to run a 
camp in the mountains (hills, to you fellas in B.C.) then he or she deliberately 
chooses to put up with weather that is rather more moist than other places. 
If you want to lift your eyes to the hills each morning, then you run the risk 
of having the rain spit right in them. Some of us have faced this and have 
chosen the mountains. We are hooked, rain OR shine. 

But moist, damp . . . let’s be honest . . . wet, summers can have several 
advantages. These may not immediately be apparent to some of you fair- 
weather-campers, so let me mention a few. 

In the first place, we almost never have to worry about sunburn, heat 
prostration, dehydration or others of that ilk v We don’t have to stock Bain de 
Soleil in our Trading Post, and as for salt pills ... we never touch ’em! Forest 
fires are not high on our list of hazards. Indeed it is the really first class counsellor 
or camper who can get a fire to go at all! The well never runs dry, and the 
lake level stays where it is, or goes higher. It was my privilege once actually 
to see my well overflow, and for several years we have had “drive-in canoe 
racks” on the beach. These advantages are not to be found in just any old 
camp, and it is well not to dismiss them too lightly. 

Roofs have to be sturdier, of course, and cabins strongly built. But, if 
they have already survived 117 inches of snow and four weeks when the tem¬ 
perature never went above 25 below (I’m talking about the WINTER, you 
understand!) then you don’t really need to worry too much about the occasional 
cloudburst which brings 6.4 inches of rain in as many minutes. 

Many changes are remarked during the summer in a rainy spot. Nostaligc 
poems about the tiny patter of rain drops on the tent roof or the smell of moist 
earth at twilight—all strong lovely stuff—have a way of disappearing from the 
bulletin board. At worst, they run the risk of being decorated by such terse 
comments as “sez you” and “oh yeah”. (Children are remarkably unimagin¬ 
ative when it comes vocabulary.) Similar poems in the Counsellors’ Bungalow 
usually have words that are unprintable here. 

The bouffant, beehive or Beatle hair-does disappear after a week of rain, 
to be replaced by the “Ouareau hair-cut”. This is rather unique, we think, 
having been done in the dark with an egg-beater. (It is considered lese majeste 
to use your right hand!) As many parents of campers and counsellors have been 
known to complain that they got the wrong child back, this now has been 
restricted to counsellors over 21. In a way it’s a status symbol! 

Our Camp Improvement Day (which is what this article started out to be 
about) was a programme which could never have been dreamed up in a camp 
which HAD SUN. It was only after six days of rain that this one appeared. 


Toronto, Canada, June 1964 


161 


Every counsellor decided what job she would dislike least in camp (this ranged 
all the way from being the Director to emptying the garbage). Actually 
several, jobs were chosen . . . such as new steps to the Tree House, painting new 
signs for the Nature Trail, stone pillars at the gate, planting 200 trees, cleaning 
the Costume Cupboard (there’s a job, if you like!) chopping firewood for 
campfires etc. 

Stealing precious time from cabin clean-up, the counsellors dreamed up 
costumes, props (in some cases, songs) to suit their particular activity. After 
Prayers and a few announcements in the Lodge, there was a sudden fanfare 
on the bugle and the entire staff paraded in with every tool in camp. Each 
group mounted the stage and gave a minute’s descriptions of what they intended 
to do to “smarten up this here camp”. It was then suggested that each camper 
could join her favourite “task force”. All Eager Beavers were give a Canadian 
Camper pin. All un-Eager Beavers were given a Heinz pickle pin to indicate 
that they were sour-pusses. (Many of these were handed back within five 
minutes.) Before you could say “knife” (en Fran^ais, naturellement) the entire 
camp was organized like the Russian army . 

The air rang to the sound of axes, hoarse cries and low pitched moans and 
groans. But when quitting whistle went there were loud cries of protest. “Who 
wants to swim? We’re having fun!” 

From that day to this Camp Improvement Day grew into C.I.W. (Camp 
Improvement Week) and heaven help any camper who didn’t join in. Juniors 
staggered back and forth with rocks. Intermediates chopped trees and stacked 
wood. Seniors buit retaining walls and run-offs (or is it runs-off?) for the 
inevitable day (tomorrows, next day, the day alter?) when it would rain again. 
Counsellors who had never done anything more arduous than conjugate “avoir” 
and “etre” suddenly found themselves working like Paul Bunyan. Campers 
puffing and panting in their plastic spacesuits (is there anything hotter than 
plastic!) were happier than clams at high tide. 

The camp sparkled, the counsellors’ morale was higher than the flag and 
the campers walked about with grins from ear to ear. Which all goes to prove 
that a little hard work is what we all need! That and a rainy summer! 

Frog Derby 

C. H. Irwin — Camp Sherwood Forest 

What to do with this rainy day? Announce at noon a Frog Derby and your 
troubles are over. Talk about an all-camp activity! 

After rest hour, rubber boots, rain coats and pails with rag covers disappear 
for the most likely frog-catching spots. You should watch this performance. 
Rain coats just hold the water IN. The captives are all handled with tender 
loving care and given the treatment of any thoroughbred just before a race. 

Certain staff members and older campers go to work on the Recreation Hall, 
arranging grandstand seats along three sides. Appropriate decorations and 
instructional signs are posted. Much thought is given to the choice of approp¬ 
riate names for steeds and jockeys in the meantime. 

At the appointed time a bugle signals the beginning of the meet and the 
stands begin to fill. Judges take their places, as do the clerks of the court and 
representatives of the S.P.C.F. (Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Frogs— 
what else?) 


162 


Canadian Camfino 



Races are called by bugle, and frogs and jockeys line up at the starting 
gate, each frog under a chocolate bar carton, each jockey armed with a 
coloured feather agitator. 

Starter’s gun can be a cap pistol or the bursting of a balloon. Boxes are 
lifted and feathers applied. Some steeds are an inch long, some weigh half a 
pound. Some leap, some hop, some just sit. Some go sideways, and the odd 
one goes straight for the finishing line. Feathers and voices are overworked, 
but he who pushes his frog is disqualified. Bedlam makes the rafters ring. Then, 
silence and the solemn announcement. The Winner! The Kitchen Boy! 

Turtle Study 

C . H. Irwin — Camp Sherwood Forest 

We all know how clearly some things can be explained and shown in 
slow-motion. It is fitting therefore that our tradtional example of slow motion, 
the turtle, should provide our nature groups with a most graphic demonstration 
of the development of the embryo. 

The large snapping turtle is common to many camping areas. Usually in 
June the female waddles out of the water in search of a sunny sandy spot in 
which to lay her eggs. These are laid in a pit, some 80 or 90 of them, about the 
size of ping pong balls. 

If the eye is kept open for likely spots, sometimes one can witness the slow 
patient excavation process, or arrive on the scene when the hole is almost full. 
At other times the tell-tale waddling trail mark leads to signs of fresh digging 
and one can discover a clutch of eggs about four inches below the surface. 
These may be left where they are or moved to a more convenient place. 
Always remember, however that they must be kept just as Nature would do, 
neither too dry nor too moist. 

Usually by the first week of camp some development has taken place. Lift 
an egg and cut the tough shell and drop its contents into a glass containing a 
little water. Pass this glass around for all to see. Do this again next week and 
the week thereafter. Soon a pulse beat will be noticed and gradually the boney 
framework will start to take shape. By the end of camp, the young turtle in the 
egg is practically complete and moving freely about, with perhaps just a small 
yolk sac still in evidence. 

For a sustained progressive demonstration this is hard to beat. 

Have you ever cooked over an almond or brazil nut? 

All you need is one shelled nut , a paper clip , clothes peg , and a small tinfoil dish . 
Unwind part of the paper clip . stick the unwound end firmly into the nut. Light the nut , 
pick up the tinfoil dish with the clothes peg, and hold it over the flame. You can cook 
an e SS> bacon cut in pieces , or anything else that will cook in a short time. 

A Trek Cart Trip! 

Kathryn Anson 
Ontario Girl Guides 

A trek cart trip is tremendous fun and allows for the younger folk not yet 
toughened to join in the trek unhampered instead of being weighed down with 
food and shelter, etc. 

There are various types of carts but a very simple one will give a lot of 
pleasure. The cart should be made to take apart. A good size is 3J4' x 2 
with detachable. sides of about 10", 2 springs with shackles, 2 bicycle wheels 
with sulky spokes and hubs and a shaft, a T bar type. A metal ring should be 


Toronto , Canada, June 1964 


163 



fastended to each axle to which ropes can be attached. These ropes are called 
tracers and two such ropes can be fastened to each shaft and affords pulling 
or braking power for the cart. Each tracer can be manned by one person and 
if the road is a tough one or a steep hill even two campers can man one tracer. 
Two campers man the shaft. A team could consist of 8 to 12 campers. This 
affords for two campers to act as a rear guard. 

As for any other trip the course must be plotted keeping in mind that the 
unimproved roads (back roads) give the best opportunities for trek carting. 
Map reading spells navigation and depending on the course 12-15 miles per 
day would be a good average. Food is a major consideration, there may be 
no means of replenishing the larder on the trip. The campers become weather 
experts or at least learn by experience and have to decide which clothes to wear, 
to pack and how to pack. Campcraft begins to live and a little physical fitness 
is considered. The team is chosen, responsibilities are sorted out and practised 
and every job is covered and a deputy standing by so that every member of the 
team has some responsibility and each camper can take his turn at every job 
and the result is that each camper is growing in Responsibility, Reliability and 
Resourcefulness. 

There is an art to packing the trek cart so that when it is loaded the 
cart will stand alone, unaided at the pulling position. There is also an art to 
pulling the cart. The tracers should never be allowed to touch the ground or 
the wheels. If the tracer is on the left then it should be pulled over the right 
shoulder and if on the right then it should be pulled over the left shoulder; in 
this way it is practically impossible for the tracers to touch the wheels. 

Portaging can be a lot of fun and the most inaccessible places explored. 
The dismantling and portaging call for a combined team spirit and effort. A new 
camp site every night and if necessary permission obtained and thanks given 
afterwards and the countryside left the better after the visit of a few campers. 
This type of tripping opens up possibilities of country wide-games, new experiences 
and the fun of a camp on the move. 

Indian Day 

E. F. Johnston—Camp Chief Hector 

For a number of years now Chief Hector has run a successful Special Event 
Day called “Indian Day.” This programme could be adapted to suit camps in 
any location and might be called “Neighbours* Day.” 

On this day we issue an open invitation to our camp neighbours — four to 
six hundred Stoney Indians — to take part in a Special Events Day with our 
campers. The programme starts in the morning with just our own campers 
learning something of the culture and customs of our neighbours, through games, 
challenge events etc. with historical costumes being worn. Shortly after lunch 
our guests begin to arrive. . turn to page 172

PROGRAMME PLANNING 


by Vincent Craven 
Pioneer Camp 


For sake of convenience, let us assume 
we are all new Camp Directors, 
anxious to do a good job of planning 
our camp programme. We have been 
around camps a great deal, but actu¬ 
ally planning the programme is a 
new experience for us. Let us con¬ 
sider a few basic principles. Someone 
or group, has to be responsible for the 
programme and here are a few ac¬ 
cepted methods: 

TO ORGANIZE THE 
PROGRAMME 

1. A Comittee of Staff & Counsellors 

This group can function before 

and after camp has begun. They 
can meet, pool and consider suggestions 
well in advance, even to the point of 
having the whole summer’s activities 
at least outlined in a general way. 
They can decide banquets, parties, 
special days, excursions, etc., with 
sufficient latitude for a necessary 
change due to weather conditions. 

2. The Campers’ Committee 

The Director has some ideas of what 
will take place, but he wants to bring 
in a democratic experience for his 
campers, so lets them plan their own 
time and activity schedule. The 
“Campers Committee” will need much 
direction and help, particularly in a 
small camp where this method can 
function quite effectively. On the other 
hand, some directors have found that 
the campers get weary of doing what 
they want, and prefer to fit into an 
already well-planned programme. 

3. The Sectional Directors’ Committee 

This group would include all section 

heads, such as waterfront, out trip, 


head counsellors, camp chaplain, sports 
director, etc. It could also include 
those who head up crafts and hobbies. 
On the other hand, it may be desirable 
not to include them all. A further 
suggestion might be to include a few 
senior campers. But the leadership and 
decisions will be made by mature and 
experienced camp people. Each person 
should be expected to come prepared 
with ideas so that time is not spent, 
wondering what we are going to do. 
This Committee can meet during the 
year as well as during the camping 
season. 

4. The Director and/or Programme 
Director 

He would obviously confer with the 
other individuals, but the responsibility 
would rest here for the summer pro¬ 
gramme. During the year, he would 
be on the lookout and thinking Pro¬ 
gramme. He will write down his ideas 
and file them for future reference. In 
this way, he would stock pile a mass 
of ideas and information, not only for 
his own use, but have it available 
when approached for ideas. This kind 
of year-round planning can be most 
helpful, when a Programme Commit¬ 
tee has been appointed, the Director 
can make suggestions “out of the hat”. 
Summary 

Whatever form the “Planning Com¬ 
mittee” responsible for the summer’s 
programme takes, one thing is certain 
and that is that preparation well in 
advance of the opening of camp is 
vital. Campers will soon detect if the 
Camp programme is not organized. 
This can lead to beefing and criticism. 


Toronto , Canada, June 1964 


165 



If the campers know there is always 
something planned, they have a feel¬ 
ing of expectancy and wonder through¬ 
out the summer. 

THE OBJECTIVE IN 
PROGRAMME PLANNING 

The oamp programme can be much 
more effective and enjoyable to all, if 
we have an objective. The waterfront 
staff, the crafts leaders, the out-trip 
department, etc., all have an objective: 
to teach campers to swim, achieve 
awards, learn to care for themselves 
in the wilderness, produce some object 
to take home, etc. However, these 
areas of camp programme are being 
dealt with in other sessions. But they 
have objectives and in every other area 
of the camp programme, there should 
be an objective. 

Whether it be a game, a drama, a 
concert, county fair, camp choir, a 
hike through the woods, or, a ball 
game, are we just filling in time, or, 
do we have an objective? There are 
ways in which we can plan our pro¬ 
gramme that the camper can learn: 

a. To participate 

b. To cooperate with others 

c. To shares responsibilities 

d. To be informed of things com¬ 
pletely new to him 

e. If nothing else it can be an ex¬ 
perience which was fun and he 
enjoyed sharing with others. 

LOCALE OF PROGRAMME 

Depending on the nature of the 
camp site and the facilities available, 
a camp programme can be planned 
accordingly. 

Wooded Area — If you have some 
bushland such activities as Wide 
Games can be planned: taking some 
historical event, selecting two teams, 
French and English, Indian Tribes, 
etc., and reacting some conflict in our 
Nation’s past. Details can be worked 
out for forts, rivers, cities, etc. Small 
paper bags filled with flour make good 
bullets or cannon shot. This kind of 


activity appeals to boys especially and 
of all ages. 

Open Field — This can be used for 
an athletic meet, with a different 
flavour and can be fun. Call it “Gre¬ 
cian Games” and all contestants must 
wear -a sheet with a laurel wreath 
around their heads. A chariot race can 
culminate the activities; these need to 
be constructed from old car axles, boat 
trailers, etc., but can be used year 
after year. 

On the Lake — Plan a sea battle, or, 
and Indian raid, with canoes and boats 
decorated or camouflaged. A float 
parade can involve a lot of people, 
use of initiative and cooperative effort, 
also, a lot of fun for participants and 
spectators and a good programme for 
visitors day. 

The Lodge or Recreation Hall — 
There arc all kinds of active indoor 
games that need not cause undue dam¬ 
age to the building. With planning, 
an effective programme can be pro¬ 
duced; i.e. a Gymnastic Display, a 
Mock Trial, a Mock Fancy Dress Ball, 
The Roman Senate in Session, dealing 
with slaves, Generals or Provincial 
Governors. The subjects and ideas arc 
unlimited and can be adapted. Dress¬ 
ing up can be half the fun. 

On the Trail — Instead of the usual 
hike through the woods, it can be 
varied by dividing into two teams, one 
trailing the other, using the accepted 
Boy Scout signs. Spies can be placed 
in the leading group. A carefully 
planned scheme can be very exciting. 
Collecting items such as insects, leaves, 
rocks, etc., can be interesting. Explain¬ 
ing a new country is most thrilling for 
younger campers. 

Planning a Work Party (A confes¬ 
sion and discovery at O.P.C.) Projects 
carefully supervised can meet a real 
need so far as older campers are con¬ 
cerned: developing camp-out sites, 
building docks, road and pathway 
construction. 


166 


Canadian Camping 



THE CAMP SING-SONG 

This is often an informal -affair but 
it can be pathetic and agonizing. To 
avoid a sing-song being a time of 
yelling, screaming, and utter confusion, 
a few points in planning a sing song 
may be helpful: 

a. Select the songs to be sung. 

b. Provide song sheets if desirable, 
printed or mimeographed. 

c. Make sure your pianist or 
other musicians can play the 
number and they have the right 
tune. 

d. Wait until everybody is ready 
and then start the music and the 
singing together. 

e. At some period during the sing¬ 
ing announce that you will be 
calling for a show of hands for 
selections. 

In this way, the sing song will be a 
well-planned and enjoyable event 
rather than something that has to be 
endured. 

PLANNED RELAXATION 

This needs planning: a cabin group 
taking a casual stroll through the 
woods; periods of reading and being 
read to; recorded music; story telling; 
table games (chess, etc). If it is well 
planned even a noisey, restless camper 
can enter in and enjoy it. 

PLANNED PROGRAMME FOR 
SPIRITUAL REFLECTION 

In every way, the spiritual should 
permeate the whole camp programme. 
The camp staff’s attitudes to the true 
values of life, should reflect in their 
conversation and actions. This will 
unconsciously impress the camper. 

Sunday Morning Chapel — This is 
important and should be well planned. 
It can be both a time of worship -and 
spiritual inspiration. A suitable guest 
speaker, who could tell something of 
the need of the “have nots” around 
the world or even in our own cities, 
can help the campers, to think beyond 
themselves. Sunday Chapel can also 


be a time of participation by coun¬ 
sellors and campers as well as a spirit¬ 
ual challenge. 

Morning and evening Devotions as 
a cabin group, can be very valuable 
and effective, providing the counsellor 
can be made to realize that it is time 
for serious reflection on the individuals 
relationship with his Creator. Suitable 
devotional booklets should be put into 
the hands of the counsellors well in 
advance. 

Breakfast Devotions, led either by 
senior staff or older campers, can be 
conducted right after the morning an¬ 
nouncements. A brief prayer for guid¬ 
ance, protection and an awareness of 
the beauty and glory of God around 
us, can give the campers a sense of 
purpose and of his own individual 
value and importance in a big world. 

INFORMAL PROGRAMMES 

These can be carefully planned, yet 
giving the campers no indication of 
their being such. 

a. Place a group of banjo or guitar 
players in a shady or comfortable 
area and let them go to it. 

b. Arrange for a pianist to be at the 
piano to play either classical or 
popular music. 

c. Get a small group started, with 
a selected person to read an ex¬ 
citing story. 

A programme thus planned may not 
necessarily last all summer, but will 
provide useful relaxation periods. It 
can be announced that Joe Doe will 
discuss a given topic with any who 
are interested, at a given place. This 
has proved effective and quite inform¬ 
al. It is possible to solicit the service 
of campers in these ideas. 

THE ELEMENT OR SURPRISE 

This in a camp programme is ex¬ 
cellent. Build up an event without 
stating exactly what it is. The feeling 
of anticipation creates enthusiasm and 
the campers enter in wholeheartedly.

Sermons! 

XHnber je H>un 

by Erik Braaten , 

Camp Pine Crest 

My subject to-day is love — a gift 
from the spirit. “Love”, you say “surely 
you can’t mean you are going to write 
about love”. Perhaps this is what 
people say when they hear the word 
“love” brought up in a conversation 
or talk. The word in the English 
language has certainly lost much of 
the meaning it once possessed. This is 
because it has acquired so many mean¬ 
ings and when you go to talk about 
love no one really knows the meaning 
you wish to express. 

We should not be proud of ourselves 
that we love or are friendly to others 
because this love is a gift from the 
Spirit. Perhaps I can clarify this idea. 
If a man made a house and gave it to 
you, you certainly wouldn’t brag and 
boast about the house by saying how 
you made it with your own two hands, 
but rather you would tell everyone how 
a real friend made this house for you, 
and you would thank your friend for 
this kind of gift. So we too should 
thank God for the great gift of love 
which he has given to us. 

Most of you know that Paul was a 
writer about 50 years after the death 
of Jesus, and he wrote during the time 
of the rise of the Christian church. 
Let’s take a more careful look at the 
first eight verses of chapter thirteen of 
Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians 
and we will learn some interesting 
points about love. 

Verse one states: “I may speak in 
tongues of men or of angels, but if I 
am without love, I am a sounding gong 
or a clanging cymbal.” Just saying lov¬ 
ing words isn’t good enough, you must 
feel them deep down inside you. You 
know the feeling of joy in yourself 
when you want to tell your Mom and 
Dad something. You might say: “Oh, 


168 


Canadian Camping 



V 


Morn I love you so much; you are 
always so good to me”. 

Verse two says: “I may have the 
gift of prophecy, and know every hid¬ 
den truth; I may have faith strong 
enough to move mountains; but if I 
have no love, I am nothing”. Prophecy 
has the power to build, to stimulate, 
and to encourage a person. One is able 
to communicate with his fellow man 
and to get across his ideas. However, 
if he doesn’t honestly love the indiv¬ 
idual he is trying to stimulate that 
communication will be lessened to no 
efTect. 

Verse three states: “I may dole out 
all I possess, or even give my body to 
be burned, but if I have no love, I am 
none the better”. In the play, “Murder 
In The Cathedral”, by T. S. Eliot, 
Becket the Archbishop, faces three 
temptations. He is tempted first to 
revert back to his lustful ways, and 
secondly he is tempted to join with 
the barons to fight against the state. 
Sir Thomas Becket shuns both these 
temptations. His final temptation was 
almost fatal for the archbishop in that 
he was begged to become a martyr. His 
reward would be the great number of 
people who would thenceforth visit 
his shrine and give him much praise. 
Sir Thomas, however, triumphed over 
this temptation too as lie said: “The 
last temptation was the greatest trea¬ 
son; to do the right deed for the wrong 
reason”. The right reason, of course, 
is acting out of love. 

I hope you are beginning to see that 
love is not a word to be avoided be¬ 
cause of its ambiguity, but one to be 
understood, practised, and used again 
and again. Paul now goes on in a 
beautiful passage, verses four to seven, 
to describe some of the key character¬ 
istics of love. 

“Love is patient”. Arc you patient 
with each boy in your cabin: when he 
is a little slow in cabin cleanup, when 
he can’t quite get that swimming test, 
when he is talking after lights out? 
Are you patient at home when someone
