canvas preservative 


Toronto , Canada , June 1964 


169 




is taking his time in a telephone booth 
or when someone is a bit late due to 
an unavoidable incident? If you are 
then you are practising love. 

“Love is kind”. Are you kind with 
the boys in your cabin? If there is a 
new boy or one who comes from a land 
far away, do you make him feel at 
home? If someone is having a hard 
time with a project, do you pitch right 
in and help? If you are kind you are 
practising love. “God sees the little 
sparrow fall”, and likewise we must 
be kind to the little creatures which 
roam this world of ours. There is a 
story told of an old hermit who lived 
up on a tall mountain shut ofT from 
civilization by deep snow. He was 
not alone though because the birds and 
animals were his friends. He could talk 
to them and they would eat from his 
hands. One day a tourist came by and 
commented on the mysterious power 
or charm this man had with the an¬ 
imals. The hermit smiled and assured 
the traveller that the only secret was 
the kindness with which he treated 
them. There is one point about kind¬ 
ness which I wish all would remember. 
Sometimes we take for granted those 
people who are close to us in our hearts 
(like our Moms and Dads and other 
relatives and our best friends). Per¬ 
haps we could remember that when 
we are with them we show our love 
for them by being kind and thoughtful 
in everything we do. 

“Love envies no one”. We should 
not be seeking those gifts which God 
has given to others, but rather be 
proud of and develop our own. Be¬ 
ginning today, why not practise that 
talent which you have been given, and 
which you know best, and don’t be 
saying: “Gee, I wish I could swim 
like him, or, why can’t I run as fast 
as he can”. 

“Love is never boastful or con¬ 
ceited”. A simple “thank you” is all 
that is necessary if someone tells you 
that you have done a good job. After 


all, God have given us our talents, and 
our part should be -a thank you to Him 
rather than walking in our own splen¬ 
dour. 

“Love is never rude”. I don’t think 
anyone is intentionally rude around 
camp, but nevertheless we must watch 
our tongues. A wise man once said 
that the tongue is the strongest muscle 
in the body because it can do so much 
damage. Sometimes the things we say 
aren’t meant to hurt people, but they 
do. You may say: “Gee, can’t we even 
joke around”. Sure you can, but think 
before you say something and see if in 
any possible way your words might 
hurt. 

“Love is never selfish”. I guess we 
all put ourselves to the foreground to 
some extent, but it is to what extent 
that counts. Giving to others brings 
joy to the giver as well as to the person 
who receives. True love is shown when 
one gives something he really wants 
for himself. It could be a piece of oake, 
a new baseball bat, or a vacation. 

“Love is not quick to take offence”. 
If a man wrongs you, you must love 
him. This is a tall order all right, but 
if you retain your anger and possibly 
look at the reasons for his attack, you 
may find that you yourself are as much 
to blame. 

Verse six states, “Love keeps no 
score of wrongs; does not gloat over 
other men’s errors, but delights in the 
truth”. Truly here we must remember 
the Lord’s prayer, “Forgive us our 
trespasses as we forgive those who 
trespass against us”. We would want 
the Lord to forgive us the errors which 
we commit, so surely we would not let 
any flame of anger bum in our own 
hearts. 

The seventh verse says, “There is 
nothing love cannot face; there is no 
limit to its faith, its hope, and its en¬ 
durance. Love will never come to an 
end”. 

There is one time of the year when 
the spirit seems to move us to per- 
turn to page 175 


170 


Canadian Camping 



frotu page 167 

To list ALL the week’s activities, on 
the bulletin board tends to produce an 
attitude of indifference. To spring a 
surprise announcement of a volley ball 
game between campers and counsellors, 
or, a Wide Game between two sections 
of camp, enthusiasm will be keen. In 
all such surprise events, the Programme 
Committees are well prepared in 
advance. 

FINAL SUGGESTION 

One final suggestion in planning the 
summer programme, diligently collect 
props and gadgets of whatever nature 
you require during the year, such as 
costumes, old clothes, rubber masks, 
etc. Many items of course can be 
made by the campers and counsellors, 
prior to the event. You may need to 
borrow a farmer’s calf, goat or rabbit, 
to be used in a programme. Make your 
arrangements ahead of time. 

Such planning and collection of 
programme material can save a direc¬ 
tor much time and effort when Gamp 
is on. As far as campers are con¬ 
cerned, the Director will be a genius 
or a magician, if he is able to produce 
what is needed at the right time for 
a programme. 

Once we become really aware of the 
need for Programme Planning, we con¬ 
tinually search for ideas and materials 
to make the programme effective. 
People have amazing ideas. Get hold of 
them! Improve them and use them! 
It’s fun!!!!!

GROWING DAYS 

O Camper-Child you may not grow 
by inches 

Through living out of doors among 

: tall trees, 

But upward-reaching thoughts should 
make you straighten 

- To match the height of sturdy 
trunks like these. 

You may not hoard the sparkle of 
the sunshine 

Though all day long you’re in 
the open air, 

But happy days of fun and merry 
laughter 

Should light your eyes with 
merry twinkles there. 

And Camper-Child, you may not 
guess that courage 

Comes oft to one who climbs some 
hilltop high, 

And faith may be for you a 
lasting dower 

If you have pondered ’neath a 
star-pricked sky. 

Maiy S. Edgar

General 

Orienteering or the use of map and 
compass is a valuable adjunct to the 
camp programme and an aid to the 
camper who may become lost. 

During electrical storms STAY OFF 
THE WATER AND OUT OF 
BOATS. NO SWIMMING SHOULD 
BE ALLOWED. 

Safe campsite selection should be 
made in family camping to ensure that 
the tent is not pitched under a large 
tree which might fall during a severe 
storm. 

Two of the most important pre¬ 
cautions for camper safety are an 
adequate swimming ability and a 
thorough knowledge of first aid. 


from page 164 

The programme is organized to include eight to ten events — archery, 
volley ball, tug-of-war, horse shoes, foot races etc. These events are used 
because they are popular with our guests and can be changed to suit the 
location of the camp. The Indian children are assigned to groups with our 
campers. The adults watch and take part in the highlight events such as a 
mammoth tug of war, archery contests, foot race etc. 

Our kitchen staff provides a supper of Bar-B-Q’d hot dogs and cake and 
punch. Following the supper our guests put on a display of their culture through 
Indian dances, songs and stories. 

We have found this to be a very effective programme in human under¬ 
standing, with our campers benefitting tremendously from their participation 
with the Indians. It has become a wonderful public relations venture as well, 
as is eagerly awaited by our guests.

mudpuppy, a large aquatic salamander 
occasionally found in the district 
(though never to my knowledge near 
the camp) was Necturus maculosus. 
This was conveniently pluralized to fit 
in with song. (Apologies to the Inter¬ 
national Committee for Rules of Zoo¬ 
logical Nomenclature.) 

After the songs, stories and presen¬ 
tations of the last fire, came the award¬ 
ing of the Mudpuppy Badge. Each 
badge, separately wrapped in smooth 
symetrically folded white Kleenex tis¬ 
sue was handed out in one hand while 
the other was shaken. The leader in a 
brief talk explained to the camp what 
a Mudpuppy was (in our sense of the 
term) and what he had to do to earn 
the badge. This came as a surprise 
to many of the campers because usually 
less than a third had been invited to 
try for the Mudpuppy Badge and those 
who had, were bidden to keep it a 
secret. 

The badge itself was made of card¬ 
board cut to the shape of an imaginary 
Necturus maculosus spattered with 
Woodland Camp Creek Mud and had 
a safety pin attached at the back. 

“Unlike other badges,” the leader’s 
voice went on, “which are worn on the 
outside to tell of the wearer’s skills or 
accomplishments, the Mudpuppy 
Badge won’t stand up to much wear. 
It only represents the real badge inside. 
This was gained during the walk up 
the creek and it will shine out for all 
to appreciate when you help others to 
see some of the interesting things of 
nature and lore of the creek.” 

Voices sighed in relief of anxious 
expectations as they heard their names 
called to receive this award. 

(I’ll tell you a little secret if you 
promise not to tell a mudpuppy:— 
“To this day no camper has ever 
failed who went with us on one of 
those delightful mud rambles up the 
creek.”)

5. The trip leader should insist on 
maintaining contact with the can¬

for all trip conditions should be 
clearly outlined. Rubber boots 
and leather boots cannot be per¬

tection are also important. If 
laced shoes are used, they ought 
to be untied while in the canoe.

purposes.

accompanying privileges arc outlined 
in the Ontario Camping Association

recognition of the need for safe prac¬ 
tices for canoeing in camps and away 
from camps while on out trips.

wasted. For many children camping 
provides the only real opportunity for

The “D” should stand for DEVp- 
TION—grace at meals, camp worship 
services. These are a privilege. In 
camp we get the right balance. We 
see the majesty and wonder of God in 
the out-of-doors. Devotion to duties— 
not shirking jobs to be done. Co-opera¬ 
tion in all activities.

ENERGY, ENTHUSIASM. There 
should be time for fun, time to rest, 
free time to read, play games, sketch 
and make friends. 

No child should go home tired out. 
Manners should improve with consid¬ 
eration for others. Campers should go 
home, healthier and happier having 
gained new skills, new interests, new 
faith in God, their neighbours, friends 
and themselves—in short, with a new 
zest for living.
